variants.name: DispatchProxy dynamic interface proxy
variants.implementation_notes: DispatchProxy.Create<TInterface, TProxy>() generates a type that implements the interface and routes every call to your overridden Invoke(MethodInfo, object?[]), so one handler adds authorization, caching, logging or fault injection to any interface without per-method forwarding code. It is the BCL's replacement for the .NET Framework RealProxy/remoting stack and covers only interfaces; Lazy<T> is the sibling BCL realization for the virtual-proxy kind. Prefer DispatchProxy when the policy is cross-cutting and the interface is stable; prefer the Lazy<T> variant when the concern is deferring construction.
pitfalls: Only interfaces can be proxied: classes need a hand-written wrapper or a bytecode proxy such as Castle DynamicProxy.
The generated proxy requires dynamic code generation, so it is flagged for trimming and NativeAOT scenarios.
Reflection dispatch wraps the subject's exceptions in TargetInvocationException; unwrap and rethrow to preserve the contract.
Generated proxy types are cached per (interface, base type); creating proxies per call wastes generation and allocation.

variants.name: Lazy<T> virtual proxy
variants.implementation_notes: Lazy<T> is the BCL's virtual proxy: the real subject is constructed on first Value access, and LazyThreadSafetyMode selects between publication-only, fully synchronized and no-safety behavior. Use it when construction is expensive and the object may never be needed; combine with DispatchProxy only if the same subject also needs per-call interception. Note that the exception from a failed factory is cached and rethrown on every later access.
pitfalls: A factory that throws poisons the instance: every subsequent Value access rethrows the cached exception - retry needs a new Lazy instance.
Lazy<T> only defers construction; it does not proxy the subject's methods, so access control still needs a wrapper or DispatchProxy.
